Sasmita Singapore’s haze crackdown tests limits of sovereignty within Asean 
 The city state has moved from conventional environmental diplomacy towards a more assertive model of cross-border corporate accountability
 3 -MIN READ 3 -MIN 1 Listen Ronny P. Sasmita Ronny P. Sasmita is a senior analyst at the Indonesia Strategic and Economics Action Institution. Published: 5:30am, 5 Nov 2026 When pollution crosses borders, sovereignty becomes more complicated. Singapore can suffer the consequences of fires burning in Indonesia, yet it cannot simply send investigators into Indonesian territory. Its attempt to hold companies accountable through domestic law has exposed a deeper dilemma in Southeast Asia: how can a region built on territorial sovereignty govern economic activities whose environmental costs routinely cross national boundaries? In October, Singapore escalated its response to the region’s recurring haze crisis. The National Environment Agency issued preventive notices to 10 Indonesian companies, followed by information requests to another 10 Singapore-based firms with plantation or forestry interests in Indonesia. It was the first time the agency had issued such information notices to Singapore-registered companies under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act since the law came into effect in 2014.
